title: Linear Momentum & Collisions
summary: Momentum $\vec p=m\vec v$ changes by impulse $\vec J=\vec F\Delta t=\Delta\vec p$. In an isolated system total momentum is conserved. Collisions are elastic (kinetic energy conserved) or inelastic (some KE lost); perfectly inelastic ones stick together.

impulse.plain: The change in momentum from a force over time.

conservation of momentum.plain: Total momentum is constant with no external force.

elastic collision.in_class: Both momentum and KE are conserved.

perfectly inelastic.in_class: Maximum KE lost; move with common velocity.

center of mass.plain: The average position of a system's mass.
center of mass.in_class: Moves as if all mass and external force were there.

recoil.plain: Backward motion when mass is ejected.

concept_sections.heading: Momentum and impulse
concept_sections.explanation: Momentum is $\vec p=m\vec v$. A force over time delivers impulse $\vec J=\vec F\Delta t$, which equals the momentum change $\Delta\vec p$.
math_steps: A longer time reduces the force for the same $\Delta p$.

concept_sections.heading: Conservation of momentum
concept_sections.explanation: With no net external force, the total momentum of a system is unchanged. Set total momentum before equal to total after.

concept_sections.heading: Elastic collisions
concept_sections.explanation: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. For two objects, this gives two equations to solve for the final velocities.
math_steps: Solve the two equations for the final speeds.

concept_sections.heading: Inelastic collisions
concept_sections.explanation: Momentum is conserved but kinetic energy isn't. In a perfectly inelastic collision the objects stick and move together at a common velocity.
math_steps: For 'stick together', one common final velocity.
KE lost = initial KE − final KE.

concept_sections.heading: Impulse and safety
concept_sections.explanation: Spreading a collision over more time reduces the peak force ($F=\Delta p/\Delta t$) — the principle behind airbags and crumple zones.

real_world_examples.title: Airbags
real_world_examples.scenario: A crash stops a driver quickly.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The airbag lengthens the stopping time, cutting the force via $F=\Delta p/\Delta t$.

real_world_examples.title: Rocket recoil
real_world_examples.scenario: A gun or rocket ejects mass.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Momentum conservation from rest gives equal-and-opposite momenta — recoil.

real_world_examples.title: Billiard balls
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A near-elastic collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy.

problems.prompt: Find the momentum of a $3$ kg cart at $4$ m/s.
A $10$ N force acts for $2$ s. Find the impulse.
A $2$ kg ball at $3$ m/s hits and sticks to a $1$ kg ball at rest. Find their common speed.
A $0.5$ kg ball hits a wall at $4$ m/s and bounces back at $4$ m/s. Find the impulse.
A $60$ kg skater throws a $2$ kg ball at $10$ m/s. Find the skater's recoil speed.
A $1$ kg cart at $6$ m/s collides elastically with an equal cart at rest. Find the final speeds.
solution_steps: Equal masses, elastic: they exchange velocities.
First stops, second moves at $6$ m/s.
